title: Designing Power: What Is Behind-the-Meter Power?
summary: Learn how behind-the-meter power adds flexibility
body_markdown:
**Why Is Behind-the-Meter Power Important for Data Centers and Large Energy Users?**


Power availability can have a direct impact on development decisions. While facilities may be designed and constructed within a few years, securing sufficient grid capacity can require significantly longer timelines. In some markets, power infrastructure timelines do not align with development schedules.


Growth in AI, cloud computing, manufacturing, electrification, and digital infrastructure is adding pressure to existing power systems. For large energy users, access to power at the right time and location can shape project schedules, site selection, and long-term investment decisions. Behind-the-meter resources provide another option for addressing power requirements when available grid capacity or utility timelines do not align with development needs.


**How Are Organizations Addressing Power Availability Constraints?**


Organizations are pursuing a range of behind-the-meter strategies based on operational requirements, local market conditions, and long-term growth objectives. Common approaches include onsite generation, battery energy storage systems, microgrids, distributed energy resources, and advanced controls that help optimize energy use.


In many cases, these technologies are integrated into broader energy strategies rather than deployed as standalone assets. Onsite generation, storage, and utility service can work together to address reliability, resilience, and capacity requirements.


For data centers, industrial facilities, and other power-intensive operations, behind-the-meter resources can provide additional flexibility when utility upgrades are delayed or available grid capacity cannot support future growth.


**What Does the Future of Behind-the-Meter Power Look Like?**


Power availability is now a significant consideration in development and expansion decisions. Behind-the-meter resources give organizations another way to plan for and address their energy requirements.


Rather than replacing utility service, onsite generation, storage, and other resources can work alongside the grid to provide greater flexibility in planning and managing energy supply. For large energy users, that flexibility can help support both near-term development and long-term energy needs.


This article accompanies the latest episode in Ameresco’s **Designing Power** video series *, “[Why Power Strategy Is Becoming a Business Strategy](https://youtube.com/shorts/Yv5VyDWmqVg?si=2F2vLEdQMB3L5tl3) .” Watch the video to learn more about how power strategy is influencing energy infrastructure planning, reliability, and long-term growth.*


What is behind-the-meter power, and why are organizations using it?


Behind-the-meter power refers to generation, storage, and energy management resources located on the customer side of the utility meter. These resources can supplement grid-supplied electricity, giving organizations greater control and flexibility in meeting their energy needs while supporting resilience.


Why is behind-the-meter power important for data centers?


Data centers require significant amounts of reliable power, but available grid capacity and utility infrastructure timelines may not align with development schedules. Behind-the-meter resources can help address those constraints by supplementing utility service and supporting both near-term power requirements and future growth.


How does behind-the-meter power work with the electric grid?


Behind-the-meter power typically works alongside the electric grid rather than replacing it. Onsite generation, storage, and other resources can complement utility service, giving organizations greater flexibility in how they manage and meet their energy needs.


Can behind-the-meter power help when grid capacity is limited or utility upgrades are delayed?


Behind-the-meter resources can supplement utility service when grid capacity is constrained or infrastructure upgrades do not align with project timelines. Onsite generation, storage, and other energy resources can be integrated based on a facility’s specific power and operational requirements.


How can behind-the-meter power support future energy needs?


Behind-the-meter resources can give organizations more options for planning and managing their power supply as energy needs change. By combining onsite generation, storage, and other resources with utility service, large energy users can support near-term development while planning for longer-term requirements.
